title: AI agent vs automation: which one you need | 50agents
description: Use an automation when the same input should always give the same result, and an AI agent when each case needs judgement. A test and a worked example.
h1: AI agent vs automation: which one you need
answer: Use an automation when the steps are the same every time, such as copying each new order into a sheet.
Use an AI agent when each case needs judgement; many jobs are an automation with one AI step.

Usually a schedule or a request
Higher, varies with what it reads

body.p: Take "keep up with new leads". An automation turns every new HubSpot contact into a row and a Slack post, but cannot tell a buyer from a student. An AI agent reads what each wrote and drafts replies to the likely buyers, which you check. Many teams run both.

method.h2: How to decide: AI agent or automation

steps.title: Write the rule as "when X, do Y"
steps.body: If you can, build an automation. "When a Stripe payment succeeds, add a row" needs no judgement, and a fixed step does it the same way every time.

steps.title: Keep anything you report on fixed
steps.body: Payroll, invoices and numbers you report on should give the same result from the same input. Keep those as automations, and add judgement only where it helps.

steps.title: Find the step that reads messy text
steps.body: Emails, tickets, web pages, notes. Reading those well is what AI is for, and usually it is one step, not the whole job.

steps.title: Put the judgement in one AI step
steps.body: Make that one step an AI step inside an automation and keep the rest fixed. Example: sort each support email into billing, bug or question, then add it to a sheet.

note.text: An AI step inside an automation costs less per run than an AI agent and fails in fewer places.

steps.title: Use an AI agent only when judgement decides
steps.body: When what to do changes case by case, build an AI agent, let it read alone, and make it ask before it sends or changes anything.

captain.line: Captain picks the kind from what you say and tells you in one line. Say "automation" and it builds one, or tells you why it cannot.
captain.ask: When a support email arrives, sort it into billing, bug or question and add it to my Support sheet

wrong.title: An AI agent where a rule would do
wrong.body: You pay for judgement on every run and get results that vary. If you can write the rule, write the rule.

wrong.title: An automation where judgement was needed
wrong.body: You keep adding filters for every exception until nobody can follow it. Move the judgement to an AI step or an AI agent.

wrong.title: Nobody can say why it did that
wrong.body: Keep an AI agent's run reports and an automation's run history, and read them. Pick tools that show both.

wrong.title: "Agentic" products that are automations
wrong.body: Some tools sold as AI agents run fixed steps. That is fine if it fits; judge them by what each run does, not the label.

faqs.q: Is an AI agent just a smarter automation?
faqs.a: No. An automation does what you set up, the same way each time. An AI agent decides what to do within its instructions, so it handles new cases and can make new mistakes.
Yes. An AI step can write an email, sort a message or pull fields out of text, while the rest of the steps stay fixed.
An automation, almost always, because it does not read and reason on every run. An AI step or an AI agent is worth its cost only where judgement saves you time.

faqs.q: How do I know a job needs judgement?
faqs.a: Try to write it as one rule: "when X, do Y". If the rule holds for every case, it is an automation. If you keep adding "unless" and "it depends", the job reads messy text or chooses, and that part needs AI.

faqs.q: Which one is easier to fix when it goes wrong?
faqs.a: An automation, because it fails loudly at one step and you can see which. An AI agent can be wrong with confidence, so keep a log of what it read and decided, and let it ask before it sends.

faqs.q: Can I start with an automation and add an AI agent later?
faqs.a: Yes, and it is the usual path. Build the fixed steps first, then add one AI step where text needs reading. Move to an AI agent only when what to do changes case by case.
